title: Clothes moth treatment
subtitle: Filled in 6 Nov 2026 from Australian museum, CSIRO and government sources, not from Mitch. Items marked in orange are for Mitch to confirm.

sections.heading: When this job comes up
body: Customer has clothes moths or carpet moths, or silverfish. Mitch's service is called Clothes Moth Treatment, and silverfish jobs have been written up as Specialist Treatment. Past invoices read: "Moth & Silverfish treatment", "Moth & Silverfish second treatment", "Carpet moth treatment" and "Rug moth treatment, 6 rugs (both sides treated)". [Mitch to confirm: does silverfish belong in this guide?]

Two clothes moths are common here and both were brought in from overseas: the case-bearing clothes moth and the webbing clothes moth. The adult moths are not what damages things. The grubs are. They go for animal fibres like wool, silk, fur and feathers. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]
The job process, the never list, PPE and the free service period are in the Every job guide. [Mitch to confirm: does the free service period apply to this job?]

sections.heading: How to tell what you have
rows: Grub living in a little silk case it drags around
Case-bearing clothes moth. Cases and droppings (frass) are the signs, for example a case inside a felt hat. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]
Creamy-white grub with a dark head, under silky webbing or tunnels
Webbing clothes moth. Fully grown it is about 12 mm. [Mitch to confirm: from WA Museum collection care manual, not from Mitch]
Small woven cases stuck to a bare wall or ceiling
Can mean pupae (the stage before the moth). [Mitch to confirm: from WA Museum collection care manual, not from Mitch]
Small moth in the wardrobe or drawers
Adults avoid light and hide in dark places like wardrobes and drawers. The case-bearing moth is about 1 cm. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum, not from Mitch]
Small, brown, hairy grub, no case or webbing
Carpet beetle. See the Carpet beetle guide. [Mitch to confirm: from Museums Victoria and Australian Museum, not from Mitch]
Wingless, shiny, scaly, with three tails
Silverfish, not a moth. Up to about 2 cm, long antennae. Eats paper, glue, cotton and other fibres. [Mitch to confirm: from Museums Victoria and WA Museum, not from Mitch]

items.a: Clothes moths. Two kinds are common here. It's the little grubs that eat the cloth, not the moths. They like wool, silk, fur and feathers. [Mitch to confirm: from Australian Museum and Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]

Moths lay their eggs on dirty cloth, and they're drawn to fabric with sweat or spilled drinks on it. They hide in dark, undisturbed spots like wardrobes, drawers and the back of cupboards. [Mitch to confirm: from Queensland Museum and Australian Museum, not from Mitch]

items.q: What can I do to help?
items.a: Keep wardrobes, drawers and storage areas clean, tidy and dust-free. Vacuum the edges of carpet, along skirting boards, under furniture and inside wardrobes. Check now and then for the first signs. [Mitch to confirm: from Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]

items.q: Is it safe for the kids and pets?
items.a: Keep kids and pets out of the area while we treat. Follow the product label for when it's safe to come back in. We normally say 1 to 2 hours once it's dry. [Mitch to confirm: from Better Health Channel (Victorian Government) and the Every job guide, not from Mitch]

items.q: Can you save my damaged wool or silk, or my good rug?
items.a: Our job is the moths. If it's a precious or badly damaged piece, a textile conservator is the one to ask before anything is done to it. [Mitch to confirm: from Queensland Museum, not from Mitch]

items.q: Is a silverfish the same thing?
items.a: No. Silverfish are a different bug. They're wingless and shiny with three tails, and they eat paper, glue and cotton. [Mitch to confirm: from Museums Victoria and WA Museum, not from Mitch]
